title: Investigator Coach (working papers): Hazira gas release and fire, 2020
audience: Investigators, HSE advisers and process-safety engineers
status: Learning purposes: not a statutory document. Derived from a ProbeMatrix investigation export; learnings are evidence-linked but should be validated by the organisation before adoption.

data_quality.text: Draft learnings from an unreviewed analysis: the export's Investigation Status is in progress and no finding is marked as edited by a person.

Working papers: whether litigation or an inquiry is in prospect is not known, so the interview plan and the follow-up table are for use only at the direction of the organisation's legal adviser, and follow-up.json is pasted back only when the adviser agrees.

bottom_line.text: Every one of the 46 evidence items comes from the enquiry committee's report; no primary record (work order, test certificate, permit, purchase record or control-system log) was seen.
Two findings quote recommendation text that the committee's report does not contain; check every quotation against the source before the findings are relied on.
No one who fitted, specified or bought the failed seal was heard: their accounts would most change the learnings on spares and return to service.
The response timeline needs reconciling: control-room clocks differed by 2 to 12 minutes, and the control-room and shift in-charge accounts disagree on when the shift in-charges were told.
The export cannot show that the investigation process met its requirements: the start date, the team and the plan to resolve and review the recommendations are not recorded.

gaps.evidence_needed: The investigation's own start record, or the office order and first site visit record.

gaps.text: The investigation team and whether a contract employee took part.
gaps.evidence_needed: The team list with each member's role and employer.

gaps.text: A system to resolve this investigation's recommendations and review them with affected personnel.
gaps.evidence_needed: The action tracker entry for each recommendation and the review plan, including contractors.

gaps.text: Primary records behind the seal change and the return to service.
gaps.evidence_needed: The work order, the test record, the purchase record for the O-ring and the return-to-service acceptance.

items.text: Absent kinds of evidence: every item is a description of the committee's report, quoting its text, photographs or CCTV frames. No primary record was examined, and several items add the analyst's reconstruction to the quote (for example the authority chain in EVD-3932), so the quote and the inference need separating.

Conflicts between sources: the report gives two years for one seal change, and the export follows the later one without a record that settles it; the gas-terminal control-room account has the shift in-charges told soon after the 02:20 alarm, while their own accounts give about 02:35; and control-room clocks differed by 2 to 12 minutes. None of the three is resolved in the export.

Quotation accuracy: two findings quote recommendations numbered D.2.iii and D.2.iv, while the committee's report has only D.2 (i) and (ii) (REC-19, REC-20); both estimate the operating pressure with no record behind it. Some evidence items give page references one page earlier than the report's text (OBS-22 and OBS-23 are on page 28).

Single-source findings: several learnings rest on one evidence item each, among them the calibration change (LR-16), the drawings (LR-19), the audit extensions (LR-21), the permits (LR-22), the fire-water pumps (LR-23) and the drill records (LR-24).
The investigation began promptly. [GAP] The export's Incident Summary has no date the investigation began; the committee's site visit dates are known only from its report.

The team included someone who knows the process, and a contract employee where contractor work was involved. [GAP] The export has no Investigation Team field; contractor work is part of the event (the drawings were made by a vendor).

The report holds the minimum fields. The export shows the incident date, a description, contributing factors (the findings) and recommendations (the register). [GAP] It does not show the date the investigation began.
A system exists to resolve the recommendations. [GAP] The export shows none for this investigation, and the site's existing tracker let audit recommendations be extended without approval.
The report will be reviewed with affected personnel, contractors included. [GAP] The export does not show a review plan; the security force and contracted agencies are among the affected.
Causes, actions and an effectiveness review are planned. Causes and proposed actions are in the findings and the register. [GAP] No effectiveness review is planned in the export.

Purchase orders and stores issue records for the meter seals since 2018; any original data sheet or drawing for the rectangular-slot gasket; any record of when, and by whom, local O-rings were adopted (the report found none).

When was the original gasket specification lost, and which function was expected to re-establish it? What did a fitter do when the original part was not in stock? Did anyone question the round O-ring in a rectangular slot?

sections.heading: Interview plan
sections.intro: For learning only, kept apart from any formal personnel process: say so at the start, offer a representative or colleague, ask what made sense at the time, and ask open questions first.

items.question: What did you have to work with when the meter seal needed replacing: parts, drawings, instructions?
items.why: The evidence holds no account from the crew; their view of the part and the test is the gap that would most change the analysis.

items.question: How was the O-ring chosen, and was it the same as on earlier jobs on this meter?
items.why: Tests whether the substitute was a crew choice or an established practice the crew inherited.

items.question: What test was normal before handing the meter back, and where did that norm come from?
items.why: Tests the hypothesis that operating-pressure checks were the accepted standard (LR-02).

items.question: Who else looked at the job before or after it was done?
items.why: Tests whether any independent check existed (LR-03).

items.question: If the right part had not been in stock, what would you have been expected to do?
items.why: Shows whether any route existed to stop the job or escalate a missing part.

items.question: How is a seal for high-pressure service specified when it is ordered?
items.why: No purchase record is in the evidence; this tests whether any specification reached procurement.

items.question: When did local purchase of these O-rings start, and who asked for it?
items.why: The report found no record of the date or authority of the switch.

items.question: What checks are done on a seal when it arrives?
items.why: Tests for any receipt inspection or quality check.

items.question: Who would you ask if an original spare could no longer be bought?
items.why: Tests which function, if any, owned re-establishing a lost specification.

items.question: How are rubber spares stored and issued?
items.why: The committee's report recommends formalising this (REC-27); the export has no finding on it.

items.question: How do you know which flameproof fittings were inspected on the last scheduled job?
items.why: The committee's report records that the fittings carried no unique identity (OBS-29); the export does not hold this, so ask how coverage is shown.

items.question: What happens to the schedule when a preventive job is delayed?
items.why: The committee's report records that a delayed job moved the next one back with no reason recorded (OBS-27).

items.question: What made the scheduled inspection due in 2020 not happen?
items.why: The committee's report records that this job was not done, with no reason recorded (OBS-28); the export holds neither.

items.question: What would a missing bolt on a light fitting look like from the ground, and who would report it?
items.why: Tests whether the defect was visible and whether a reporting route existed.

items.question: What does the team need to inspect every fitting, not only the failed ones?
items.why: Points the learning at resources and records, not at the people doing the work.

items.question: How was the hydrocarbon-leak scenario in the plan written, and by whom?
items.why: The plan names the scenario but gives no isolation decision; this asks how that came about.

items.question: Who does the plan expect to decide on isolating a trunk-line supply at night?
items.why: Tests the delegated-authority hypothesis behind LR-07.

items.question: How are drill findings fed back into the plan?
items.why: Drill records held no observations or actions (LR-24).

items.question: What would make the night shift confident to isolate without waiting for senior posts?
items.why: Asks for the system change, not for individual judgement.

items.question: Which other scenarios in the plan stop short of the isolation decision?
items.why: Tests whether the gap is specific to this scenario or general.

items.question: Before these learnings are published: does this account match what you saw, knew and were trying to do that night, and what is missing from it?
items.why: Validates the account with the people involved before learnings are shared.

items.text: Where the analysis reached levels 3 and 4: it climbed from the seal substitution as an act (level 1) through supervision that let it become normal (level 3) to the absence of any function owning the specification (level 4). The same climb is visible for the pressure test, the isolation decision and the detection design.

Findings coded too low: some level-1 findings describe a crew or shift decision where the cause is organisational, such as the missing pressure test, which no procedure required, and the delayed isolation, which the plan gave no criteria for. Read them with their level-4 counterparts, and keep the lesson at the level of the cause.

Hindsight wording: several finding labels describe the response as a failure to act on information. Rewrite them with the knowable-then test: what each role knew, from whom, and what the plan asked of them at that moment.
Check every quotation against the source before publishing: an AI-assisted analysis can attribute text to a report that the report does not contain.

items.situation: FND-212DC9B7 codes the missing pressure test after the seal change as the crew's decision, at level 1.
prompts: What did the crew have to go on: a procedure, a test standard, a known design pressure?
At which level does 'no procedure required the test' belong?
Rewrite the label so it passes the knowable-then test.

items.situation: FND-7A32AC87 quotes a committee recommendation numbered D.2.iii.
prompts: Find the recommendation in section 12 of the committee's report.
What does the report actually recommend on spares (sections E.1 to E.3)?
How would you correct the finding, and who must agree the change?

items.situation: Control-room clocks differed by 2 to 12 minutes, and two sources disagree on when the shift in-charges were told of the release.
prompts: Which records would fix the true times?
How would you show uncertain times on the timeline?
Which learnings change if the shift in-charges were told earlier?

limits: The export is a desk analysis of the enquiry committee's report; it holds no site evidence, interviews or primary records of its own.
The privilege question could not be put to the organisation for this public sample, so the pack is titled working papers.
